analysis.one_liner: Requires streaming services to warn viewers on-screen before collecting video or audio from their viewing area.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a House floor vote and died at the end of the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Some video services — like TVs and streaming devices with cameras or microphones — can collect sights and sounds from the room while you watch. The bill would have prohibited that unless the service displayed a 'We are watching you' message on screen, explained what it collects and why, offered an identical no-surveillance version of the service, and got your consent before sharing anything. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules. The bill never advanced past its first committee assignment in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who use video streaming services and devices: they would get an on-screen notice whenever their camera or microphone was being used, a plain description of what is collected, a service option with no surveillance built in, and a rule that collected information can only be shared with their consent or by court order.

how_it_helps.text: Bars video services from collecting visual or audio information from around the viewing device unless they display a continuous on-screen 'We are watching you' message and describe what is collected and how it is used.
Requires operators to offer an otherwise-identical version of the service with no such collection, and, for operator-provided devices, hardware that cannot collect the information at all.
Limits sharing of collected information to cases of the consumer's express consent or a court order tied to a law enforcement investigation.
Makes violations enforceable as unfair or deceptive practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act, with FTC rulemaking to implement the requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Video service operators — streaming providers, cable and satellite companies, and makers of smart TVs and other viewing devices — would bear compliance costs, lose the ability to freely gather viewing-area audio and video, and would have to supply surveillance-free service options and hardware.

drawbacks.text: The one-time on-screen disclosure and continuous 'We are watching you' banner could be easy for viewers to ignore or dismiss, so the bill relies heavily on notice rather than restricting collection outright — a service could still watch and listen as long as it told you.
Operators would face real compliance costs, including building or sourcing devices incapable of collection for the surveillance-free option, which could add expense to equipment and services.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protection is meaningful but narrow: it covers only the video services it defines and leans on disclosure and an opt-out service rather than an outright ban on collection. For consumers, the cost is negligible and the protection is real, particularly the consent requirement before sharing recordings. The main weakness is that a banner and a terms-of-service paragraph may not do much to change behavior when the alternative is losing the service.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 27, 2017 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On February 3, 2017 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Digital Commerce and Consumer Protection, which was its last recorded action.
The bill attracted six cosponsors (five Democrats and one Republican) but never advanced to a vote in either chamber before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Video service operators and smart-device makers, who avoided any new limits on collecting audio and video from viewers' rooms; consumers gained nothing because the protections never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Video services that collect viewing-area data

for.name: Rep. Michael Capuano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

for.name: 5 House Democrats and 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it nominal bipartisan support.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in subcommittee referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's six cosponsors split five Democrats and one Republican, but no vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of opposition is unknown from the record.

industries.industry: Streaming video, cable, and smart-TV/device operators
industries.note: The bill would have barred them from collecting video and audio from viewers' rooms without an on-screen warning, forced an identical surveillance-free service option, and required consent before sharing anything. Its death left the industry free to gather viewing-area data with no federal notice or choice requirements.
Viewing-area audio and video is valuable for targeting ads and profiling households; the consent-before-disclosure rule would have cut off much of that resale. Nothing changed because the bill died.
